source_group: Modern field surveys of Adivasi astronomy
summary_findings: Five modern field surveys, covering eleven communities that the printed record of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries does not reach at all. tribal.json was built from colonial lexicography and ethnography and could name only five communities with a sky nomenclature deep enough to call a system; this file adds the Banjara, the Kolam, the Korku, three Nicobar island communities and the Bhil, Mavchi Bhil, Vasave Bhil, Pawra and Kokna, all recorded between 2013 and 2023 by teams working village by village with a questionnaire. Every one of these papers is in copyright, so every entry here is paraphrased and every `quote` is null, on the footing tribal.json already established for its twenty Gondi entries. THE FOUR THREADS tribal.json IDENTIFIED ALL HOLD, AND ONE OF THEM GETS SHARPER. (1) THE COT: the Big Dipper is a cot in Kolami (Mandater), a cot of the DEAD in Lambadi (Jamakhat, from Yama), a hen-basket on Chowra (Lonob) and a COFFIN on Teressa (Rohiung), and the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna all have the cot with its leg pulled crooked by a thief. Lambadi is Indo-Aryan, Kolami and Bhili are Dravidian and Indo-Aryan respectively, Korku is Munda, Nicobarese is island Austroasiatic — and the death sense, which tribal.json found only in Mundari's bier, now appears three times in unrelated languages. (2) THE THIEVES: three of them, everywhere, but WHO they are is local. Korku numbers them (Pahila, Dusara, Tisara chor); the Kolams make them a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan; the Bhils make them the village elder, the chief, the sheriff and the revenue collector. The figure is shared, the cast is politics. (3) ORION IS AN IMPLEMENT, NOT A HUNTER: a seed drill for the Kolams (Tipan) and the Bhils (Pambar), a full plough with two bullocks and a ploughman for the Korku (Harnangar, Doba 1, Doba 2, Nangarnara manus). The single exception is the Banjaras, a trading people, who keep the mainstream deer (Halni) and, the paper notes, barely look at Orion otherwise. (4) THE MILKY WAY IS A ROAD WITH ANIMALS ON IT: Kolam Margam 'an animal path', Banjara Mardaar wat 'the path of the dead or of animals', Bhil and Mavchi 'the path of cows'. The Nicobarese are the exception the earlier file already predicted: on Camorta and Teressa it is a spring of water. THE BIRD AND ITS EGGS, which tribal.json called a subtler fourth thread, turns out to be the most productive figure of all. Kolam Kovela Kor is the Pleiades as one large bird and several small ones, Kolam Bhori is Aldebaran the bird with two eggs, Korku Pankheru is Sirius the bird with Bhori Aakom its eggs — the same word Bhori in a Dravidian and a Munda language — and among the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna a single bird named hulgi carries Orion's Belt, the Pleiades and a triangle of Auriga as its eggs in different villages. The figure is stable; the stars it lands on are not. TWO OTHER RESULTS. Kolam Irukmara, the Mahua tree at Crux with an old woman and a young woman gathering its flowers beneath it, is almost certainly the same word as Gondi Irukna Mara, which tribal.json had to record as unidentified for want of a modern equivalent; this file does not alter that entry but the two should be read together. And the Bhil Milky Way at Varpada is a kinship rule drawn on the sky: the band forks because a woman meeting her husband's elder brother on the road must turn aside, and the avoidance is a real rule of conduct in these communities. NEGATIVE AND UNOBTAINED. The Banjara pole star, which this summary previously recorded as identified but unnamed, is named twice in the paper's appendix as Dhruv Tara and is now entered — the negative finding was true of Table 1 and false of the paper, and it is corrected here rather than quietly dropped; no name is claimed for none for the Korku words for comet and meteor, which the paper describes ('a broom star', 'stellar excreta') without printing; and none for the Korku Lupus figure, for which only the English gloss 'Tree of Mahua' is given. The second-hand Nicobarese lists quoted inside the 2018 paper from Rajamanickam (1997) and Justine (2013) — Onchiana for Centaurus, Thyan for Orion, Mahayuvan for Crux, Musaha for Ursa Major, Gna-gna-hyaam for the Pleiades, and Justine's Chowra and Kondule constellation lists — are NOT entered: they are transcriptions at second hand, and this database does not rest an entry on those. They are the obvious next thing to chase. Three further papers of the same programme were not obtained and no entry is offered from them: the Pardhi study, the Cholanaikkan study, and the Warli, Dhodia, Katkari and Kokna study. THIRTY-SIX BANJARA AND KOLAM ENTRIES ADDED ON A LATER PASS from the village appendices of the 2014 paper, pp. 77-84. The largest single gain is the compass: six Banjara quarters and four Kolam ones, where the Banjara north is Dongari, 'the hills' — the same word the Pardhi use, in this same file — and the two Kolam villages that gave the quarters swap north and south between them, which is recorded as disputed rather than resolved. The Kolam rainbow Ayak is the grandparents, the grandfather standing at the violet end and the grandmother at the red, the only name in this database that divides a sky object by colour and puts a person at each end. The five animals around Samdur that gauge the coming monsoon are named at last — Namli the peacock, Barre the buffalo, Pande the frog, Mekam the deer, Gurram the horse, and a sixth, the pig Ture — with the recorders' suggested constellations carried as disputed because the suggestions are theirs and not the informants'. Kavadi Kunde, the tower of three pots, is Cygnus in most villages and Orion's Belt in two, and the paper says so itself. And the Banjaras see an old woman, yadi, spinning cotton under a banyan tree in the face of the Moon — the only reading of the lunar maria anywhere in these fifty-seven languages.

THE COT AGAIN, AND EXPLICITLY A DEATH-COT. tribal.json identified the cot as the one figure shared across unrelated families (Santali buḍhi parkom ipil, Kurukh khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō, Gondi Sedona Katul, Chhattisgarhi Dhuri); Mundari alone turned it into a bier. Lambadi is Indo-Aryan, unrelated to any of those, and its name carries the death sense in the word itself — yama/jama being the god of the dead.

THE THIEVES, BUT NOT THIEVES. Everywhere else in this database the three handle stars are thieves at the cot — Santali, Kurukh, Gondi, Chhattisgarhi Dhuri, and the Bhil and Pawra entries below. The Kolams instead make them one man of each of the three communities who share their landscape, with the Pardhan chief at the end. No Kolami words are printed for the three, so none is invented here; the entry is kept because the identification itself is the finding. Compare the precedent of the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json, likewise entered without a vernacular form. CORRECTED: this entry previously carried no vernacular form, on the ground that Table 2 prints the identification without a word. The appendix prints the word twice — Chinchpod gives the cot Ter and the thieves Dongal, and Raipur gives three thieves, Dongal, a Kolam, a Gond and a Patadi. The bracketed placeholder has been replaced by the name and the caveat about nameless entries no longer counts this one.

caveats: EVERY SOURCE IN THIS FILE IS IN COPYRIGHT AND NOTHING IS QUOTED. All five papers date from 2013-2023. The findings are paraphrased, the page is cited, `quote` and `quote_lang` are null throughout, and the wording of the glosses is the recorders' own only where a gloss is a single word or a fixed phrase for which no paraphrase is possible. This is the convention tribal.json set for its Gondi entries and it is followed here without exception.

The Greek letters are unrecoverable from the Korku paper. The ADS scan of JAHH 19(2) renders every Greek glyph as a solid black box — in the page image, not merely in the extracted text — so 'Rigil Kent (α Cen)' reads as 'Rigil Kent ( Cen)'. Where the paper also prints the star's proper name the Bayer letter is unambiguous and has been restored (Alioth = ε UMa, Alnitak = ζ Ori, and so on). Where it prints only the lost letter and a constellation, nothing is restored: Bharada and Patni are graded 'unidentified', Pati 'unidentified' with its magnitude also garbled in the source, and Miryan 'likely' on a magnitude-and-position argument that is stated in its notes and not written into modern_star.

The Bhil paper could not be read as text at all. Its embedded font subsets carry no ToUnicode map, so extraction yields a monoalphabetic substitution cipher — and a different cipher per font, so the running heads, the body and the table captions each scramble differently. Every Bhil, Pawra, Mavchi, Vasave and Kokna reading in this file was read off a rendered page image at 150 dpi. Nothing was decoded by solving the cipher, because a cipher solved against English prose is not evidence for the spelling of a Bhili word.

THREE entries carry no vernacular name and are kept anyway: the Bhil cot; the Mavchi Bhil Pleiades as girls crushing grain; and the Bhil Milky Way as the road of Jeth and the daughter-in-law. In each the paper reports the figure in detail but prints no vernacular word for it. The precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json. An identification without a name is a weaker record than a name with an identification, and the `name_roman` field says so in plain words rather than carrying an invented form. THIS CAVEAT USED TO SAY FOUR. The fourth was the Kolam identification of the three trailing stars as a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan, which the summary tables give without a word — but the appendix names them Dongal, and that entry now carries the name.

Village counts are reported where the papers give them, because they are the best measure of how firmly held a figure is: the Korku cot and thieves are in all twelve villages surveyed, Kolam Kovela Kor in all ten, Banjara Jamakhat in all six, while Banjara Kamedi, Kolam Sappa and Kolam Danedare Pila rest on one or two villages each and are graded accordingly. A name from one village is not the same kind of fact as a name from twelve.

The `region` field gives the district or island where the fieldwork was done, not a claim about the whole speech community. These surveys sampled particular villages, and the papers themselves show the same community differing village by village — the Kokna call the Pleiades a heap of hay in one village and a long-tailed bird in another.

iso639_3 codes are assigned by the compiler from the community name the papers use, and the papers do not give codes. Lambadi (lmn), Kolami (kfb), Korku (kfq), Bhili (bhb), Mavchi (mvf), Vasavi (vas) and Kukna (kex) are straightforward. Two are less so: 'Pawra' is taken as Pauri Bareli (bfb), and the three Nicobar localities are assigned Central Nicobarese (ncb) for Camorta, Chaura (crv) for Chowra and Teressa (tef) for Teressa on the basis of the island named. Where a reader disagrees, the region field carries the fact and the code does not.

Cross-references in the notes to tribal.json name the parallel and do not merge the entries. Kolam Irukmara and Gondi Irukna Mara are almost certainly the same word, and this file identifies it as Crux; the Gondi entry keeps its 'unidentified' grade, because one community's identification of a cognate is evidence about the other and not proof. The same restraint applies to Banjara Medi, Kolam Met and Korku Miryan, three threshing-pole names on three different stars.

The register is `tribal` for every entry except two: Banjara Chanda for the Moon and Korku Dhur tara for the pole star, both tagged `sanskritic` because the recorders themselves flag them as close to the Sanskrit. That is their judgement, not the compiler's, exactly as with the four sanskritic tags in tribal.json.

THE PARDHI PAPER WAS OBTAINED ON A LATER PASS and closes one of the three gaps this file recorded. ADS serves the full-text scan free at articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/2019JAHH...22..179H. Its text layer is partly a substitution cipher, as the Bhil paper's is — every italic and bold word extracts as a uniform shift of the alphabet — so the tables were read off page images rendered at 165 dpi, and the cipher was not solved. The remaining gap in the programme is the Warli / Dhodia / Katkari / Kokna study, which appears not to have been published: a public talk abstract summarises its findings in English (the Katkari Big Dipper as a cot with Koli, Warli and Konkana trailing it; Orion's Belt a bow and the sword an arrow; the Pleiades a big drum; Taurus a wedding procession), but a web summary of a talk is not a citable transcription and no entry rests on it.

The Pardhi survey is the only one in this file whose informants are not cultivators, and the authors' own argument turns on it: eleven of the fourteen villages live by hunting and scavenging, the three Gav Pardhi villages took to farming under British rule less than a century ago, and the two vocabulary tables contain no farming word at all. Their conclusion is that the terminology was fixed while all Pardhi were hunter-gatherers. This database's own cross-family pattern — that Orion is an implement and never a hunt — is the mirror of that argument, and the Pardhi are its one exception.

Village counts quoted in the usage notes are from the paper's Table 3, which tables each belief against the fourteen villages it was collected in. No other source in this file, and none elsewhere in this database, reports how many informants held a belief; where the count is given it is quoted, because 'thirteen of fourteen villages' and 'one village' are very different claims and a name-list flattens them.

The Pardhi were gazetted a Criminal Tribe in 1871 and the stigma outlasted denotification; the authors say so at length and connect it to the community's isolation. Two entries name living surnames and their family goddesses. They are reproduced because the paper prints them as the content of the star-names, and for no other reason.

THE SOURCE THAT PROMPTED THIS PASS, AND WHY IT IS NOT CITED ON A SINGLE ENTRY. M.N. Vahia, Nisha Yadav and Srikumar M. Menon, 'Perspectives on Early Astronomy in Indian Context' — an unpublished book manuscript prepared for the National Council of Science Museums, version 2 revision 5, PDF dated 11 July 2017, 111 pages, supplied privately and in copyright. Its section 4.1, 'Astronomy of some Indian tribes' (pp. 54-58), sets the Banjara, Kolam and Gond skies side by side in two tables. Every name in those tables is drawn from the authors' own two field papers, Vahia & Halkare 2013 and Vahia, Halkare, Menon & Calamur 2014, which this compilation already cited — so the book is a secondary condensation of sources already held, and citing it for a name it did not first print would put the wrong source on the record. What the book did do is show that this compilation had taken the two papers from their summary tables alone: the book's Gond column carries names for the Sun and the Moon that were not here, and its Kolam column a rainbow that was not here. Re-reading both papers end to end after that, including the village-by-village appendices the book condenses away, produced forty-seven further entries and four corrections. THE BOOK IS THEREFORE THE REASON FOR THE PASS AND THE SOURCE OF NONE OF IT, and is credited here rather than in the citation field. Nothing from it is quoted; it is in copyright and unpublished, and the material taken is in any case the papers'.

TABLES ARE NOT THE PAPER. Both Vahia papers put their findings in a summary table and then print a village-by-village appendix, and the appendix carries names the tables never show: the Banjara pole star, the six quarters of the Banjara horizon, the Kolam rainbow's two grandparents, the names of the five rain-animals around Samdur, the word Dongal for the Kolam thieves. This compilation's first pass worked from the tables, and four of its statements were wrong as a result — three entries said no vernacular form was printed when one was, and the summary claimed a negative finding about the Banjara pole star that the appendix refutes. All four are corrected in place and each correction says so in its own notes rather than being silently overwritten. The lesson generalises to every field paper in this file.
